Chapter 8. The Politics of Respectability: Navigating Expectations
You ever feel like someone’s always watching, just waiting to judge every little thing you do? For Black women, that pressure isn’t just in their heads—it’s a real, daily force. There’s this thing called “respectability politics.” It’s that idea that, if you just act right—dress a certain way, talk a certain way, basically follow all these unspoken rules—maybe, just maybe, you’ll earn respect or stay safe.
Picture a mother gently reminding her daughter to dress modestly, to always speak with perfect manners, and never give anyone a reason to look down on her. The hope here is simple: if you follow the rules, you’ll be spared from harm. But life’s not that simple, is it? Even if you do everything “right,” the world can still turn on you—discrimination or violence can show up, uninvited, no matter how careful you are.
What most people don’t see is just how exhausting it is to live under this microscope. Imagine every choice—what you wear, how you talk, even who you love—suddenly loaded with meaning. One misstep, and it’s not just you who’s judged; sometimes, people use it as an excuse to treat a whole community unfairly.
So, what do you do? Some women try to fit the mold, hoping for a little safety or maybe some approval. Others push back, deciding they’re going to be themselves—imperfections and all. And honestly, neither road is easy. Each comes with its own risks and rewards.
The toughest part? Trying to live authentically, to be true to yourself, without letting the weight of everyone else’s expectations crush you.
After a while, it becomes clear: respectability is a moving target. It shifts and changes, and too often, it divides people instead of protecting them.
Real freedom is about defining yourself—no apologies, no fear. And that’s something worth holding onto.
